lede: AI funding worries hit Asian chipmakers (Kospi down more than 5%); Nasdaq futures -0.6%; oil eases; big banks report today.
geo_headlines: THE CHIP SELLOFF SPREAD TO ASIA. South Korea's Kospi fell more than 5% to below 6,000, its lowest since July 31, and Japan's Nikkei fell 2.6% (investingLive). SK Hynix fell more than 10%, SoftBank 8.5%, Samsung 7.4% and Tokyo Electron 7.2% (CNBC). **The triggers were warnings from the Intel and Broadcom CEOs that access to capital could become a major headwind for the AI boom, plus a memory-chip advance by China's CXMT (CNBC).**

FUTURES LOWER; NASDAQ LEADS. Nasdaq 100 futures 30,718.75 (-0.58%) and S&P 500 futures 7,848.75 (-0.12%) as of 6:55 AM ET. Monday the Nasdaq 100 fell 0.71% and chips 2.67%, while the Dow rose 0.38%; the S&P 500 slipped 0.06% to 7,807.24, 0.15% below its October 6 record close. Micron fell 3.9% (CNBC).

OIL EASED; SAUDI PIPELINE PLAN. Brent December $104.59 (-1.9%) and WTI November $91.76 (-2.1%) after Monday's 2% rally. Saudi Arabia is studying raising pipeline crude export capacity to 10 million barrels a day, bypassing Hormuz, with 1.2 million added within seven to eight weeks (investingLive). UKMTO counted six vessel strikes in and near the Strait on Sunday (The National).

HOUTHIS: AIRLINES PULL BACK. Trump said the Houthis are "misbehaving very badly" after attacks on Riyadh and Dammam airports. Saudi Arabia halted flights at Riyadh, and Air France-KLM, Lufthansa, Qatar Airways and others suspended service (Al Jazeera).

FED: HAMMACK SEES BROAD INFLATION. Cleveland Fed President Hammack said Monday inflation pressures are broad-based and restrictive policy is needed (Barchart). NFIB small-business optimism fell to 97.9 from 98.7 (98 expected) (Dow Jones). FedWatch, as of Friday 10/9: October hike 18.8%, December 84.3%.

TODAY: BIG BANKS REPORT. JPMorgan and Wells Fargo release at about 7:00 AM; JPMorgan call 8:30 AM (consensus EPS $5.90-5.93), Goldman 9:30 AM ($13.02), Wells Fargo 10:00 AM ($1.85), Citi 11:00 AM ($2.66) (CNBC, company releases). Treasuries reopen after the holiday. Wednesday 8:30 AM: September CPI.
client_frame_short: The AI scare is back, and this time it started overseas. South Korea's market fell more than 5% overnight after the Intel and Broadcom CEOs warned that financing could become a bottleneck for AI spending, and US Nasdaq futures are down about 0.6%. **This is a correction inside a strong market, not a break: the S&P 500 is 0.15% below its record, and the Dow rose Monday.** Today's bank earnings and Wednesday's inflation report matter more for most portfolios than one rough night in Seoul. For clients, no changes are needed.
client_frame:
If a client calls this morning, the story is AI nerves, again, while the rest of the market holds up.

What happened: on Monday, the CEOs of Intel and Broadcom warned that access to capital could become a major headwind for the AI build-out, and a Chinese memory maker announced a technical advance. Chip stocks fell 2.7% in the US. Overnight that spread to Asia: Korea's market fell more than 5%, with SK Hynix down more than 10% and Samsung down 7.4%, and SoftBank, a big OpenAI investor, fell 8.5%.

The context: AI stocks have had a huge run and a lot of spending riding on them, so they are sensitive to any hint that the money could slow. This is the second scare in a week, after Thursday's report on OpenAI's revenue.

The rest of the market: the Dow rose Monday and the S&P 500 is 0.15% below its record. Analysts expect third-quarter S&P 500 profits to rise about 25%, up from 22% in July (Bloomberg Intelligence).

Oil eased to about $105 Brent. Saudi Arabia is studying a pipeline expansion to move more crude around Hormuz, which would ease the supply squeeze over time.

Today: JPMorgan, Goldman, Wells Fargo and Citi report. Then Wednesday's CPI, expected at 3.6% headline and 2.5% core.

Why it matters: concentration risk is the real lesson. Portfolios tilted heavily toward AI and chips feel these weeks much more than diversified ones. That argues for regular rebalancing, not for selling. A client who has let a few big tech winners grow into an outsized share of the account is the right person to call this week.

For clients, the message holds: high-quality bonds pay more than 5% for a decade, and long-term equity plans do not need changing. What would change the view: a 10-year close above 5.40% (Friday 5.24%), a 30-year above 5.75% (Friday 5.60%), or US strikes on Iran that keep Brent well above $105 (now $104.59).
